question: Does upgrading the installed packages under a live account keep the settings, the credential and the work in progress -- and does going back to the older version refuse cleanly rather than damage what the newer one wrote?
why_now: M6 line 328 asks exactly this and has never been testable: it needs a machine with a real account and credentials in a keyring, installed from packages rather than from a developer build. The Fedora VM became that machine on 2026-09-14. A package upgrade that quietly loses a credential costs the person a browser sign-in; one that loses pending work costs them a file.
how: The Fedora VM currently runs 0.1.0~dev.r409.ge24da99 installed from rpm, with the owner's OneDrive connected read-only, one pinned file resident, and the credential in an unlocked login keyring. It is upgraded with dnf to the rpm CI builds for the current tree, then rolled back to r409 with dnf downgrade. Nothing is signed in again at any point; needing to would itself be the failure.

predictions.P1: The upgrade replaces both packages and the account is still there afterwards, mounted, with no sign-in required. The credential is in the keyring, not in the package, so nothing the package manager does should reach it.
predictions.P2: The pin survives with its bytes still resident, because pins live in the state directory under ~/.local/state/cirrove, which no package owns.
predictions.P3: Exactly one copy of the Files extension exists afterwards. This is the failure that has actually happened on this project before -- a home-installed copy beside a packaged one made Files load both and show every badge and menu item twice.
predictions.P4: The running daemon is restarted by the upgrade or keeps running on the old binary until it is; either is acceptable, but it must not end up serving a mount from a deleted binary, and the mount must not be left behind after the daemon goes.
predictions.P5: The new tray mark is in place and the tray advertises it, since this upgrade is also the first packaged build carrying the redrawn icons.
predictions.P6: The downgrade is the one most likely to be wrong. An older binary meeting a state directory a newer one has written should refuse to read it and say so, not silently reinterpret it -- cirrove-service already refuses a settings file from a newer version in its unit tests, and this is that path meeting a real rollback. If it instead starts and reports no accounts, that is a person's drive apparently vanishing after a rollback.

run.where: Fedora 44 VM, GNOME Wayland, SELinux enforcing. From 0.1.0~dev.r409.ge24da99 to r418.gfb24186 and back, both rpms built by CI, with the owner's OneDrive connected read-only and one 66 KB file pinned. No sign-in at any point.

observed.P1: HOLDS. Both packages upgraded, the account is still there, still mounted, still ready with all 184053 items, and nothing asked for a sign-in.
observed.P2: HOLDS. The pin survived with its 66 KB still resident, and the credential id in accounts.json is byte-for-byte the one from before (ec68eb67). The credential is in the keyring, which no package owns.
observed.P3: HOLDS. Exactly one copy of the Files extension afterwards.
observed.P4: FAILS, and this is the finding. The daemon's pid was 3372 before the upgrade and 3372 after it, with /proc/3372/exe pointing at '/usr/bin/cirroved (deleted)'. The tray likewise. An rpm upgrade replaces the files and leaves the old processes running from the unlinked inodes, so a person who upgrades keeps running the old version indefinitely -- until they log out, reboot, or restart the unit by hand. Nothing tells them. The mount stayed healthy throughout, so nothing is broken; what is wrong is that the upgrade did not take effect and said nothing about it.
observed.P5: HOLDS, once the services are restarted. After restarting the daemon and the tray, the redrawn mark is in Fedora's top bar, white and monochrome beside the network, volume and power icons -- which is the desktop and the exact complaint that prompted the redraw. Before the restart the old tray was still advertising the old icon, which is P4 seen from the user's side: you upgrade and the new icon does not appear.
observed.P6: The bad outcome did not happen, but the guard was not exercised either. dnf downgrade to r409 succeeded, the older daemon started, found its account, mounted, reported all 184053 items and still knew the pin. Nothing was refused because nothing needed to be: r409 and r418 write the same state format, so this rollback never met a newer schema. The refusal path -- cirrove-service refuses a settings file from a newer version, which its unit tests cover -- remains untested against a real rollback, and will stay that way until a release actually changes the format. Recorded as not proven rather than as proven.

run.not_covered: Pending work. The account here is read-only, so there were no queued uploads to protect across the upgrade, and 'protects pending work' is the third of the row's three nouns. That needs a write-consented account with something deliberately stuck in the journal, which the Ubuntu VM could do after its measurement window closes.

conclusion: An upgrade under a live account keeps the settings, the credential and the pinned content, and a rollback keeps them too. One real defect: the upgrade does not restart the daemon or the tray, so both keep running from deleted binaries and the person stays on the old version without being told -- visible as the new icon simply not appearing. Two things are recorded as unproven rather than passed: the newer-state refusal, because these two builds share a format, and pending work, because this account is read-only. UPDATE 2026-09-14: pending work is now covered too, on the Ubuntu VM with write consent. Three uploads queued against an unreachable provider survived the package upgrade, survived a restart onto the new binary, finished 52 seconds after the provider returned with nobody retrying them, and were read back through a different machine's mount of the same drive. stuck_changes stayed zero throughout, which is the distinction that matters: waiting is not stuck. All three nouns of the row -- settings, credentials and pending work -- are now measured rather than assumed.

second_run_pending_work.question: Does an upgrade protect work that has not reached the cloud yet -- the third noun in the row, and the one the first run could not touch because its account was read-only?
second_run_pending_work.how: The Ubuntu VM, whose account has write consent. The link is pulled with QMP so the provider is unreachable, files are written into the mount so they queue in the upload journal, and the packages are upgraded from r370 to a current build while those uploads are still queued. Then the link is restored and the queue is watched. Every file is named as a Cirrove upgrade check and removed to the recycle bin afterwards.

predictions.Q1: The queued uploads survive the upgrade. They are in the journal under ~/.local/state/cirrove, which no package owns, so nothing dpkg does should reach them -- but the row exists because that is the assumption worth testing rather than asserting.
predictions.Q2: They finish once the link returns, without anyone retrying them by hand, and the files are really in the cloud rather than merely marked done. Confirmed by reading them back through a second machine's mount of the same drive, not through the daemon that uploaded them.
predictions.Q3: stuck_changes stays zero throughout. An upload waiting for a provider is pending, not stuck, and reporting it as stuck would send someone to discard work that was about to succeed.
predictions.Q4: The upgrade does not restart the daemon -- already measured on Fedora -- so the queue is carried by the same process. The interesting case would be the queue surviving a restart as well, which the journal is designed for and which this run also exercises by restarting onto the new binary while items are still queued.

result.when: 2026-09-14T17:19-17:23+02:00, the Ubuntu VM, r370 to r409 with the account's write consent
result.how_the_provider_was_made_unreachable: Not by pulling the virtual cable, which was tried first and cut ssh with it -- the machine's only channel runs over the same user-mode network. Blocking outbound tcp/443 from inside does the job instead: the provider becomes unreachable while the machine stays drivable, because ssh arrives from the gateway rather than leaving for it.

observed.Q1: HOLDS. Three files written with the provider unreachable queued as pending and verifyrequired, and all six journal entries naming them were still there after apt-get install replaced both packages.
observed.Q2: HOLDS, and by the stronger route. 52 seconds after tcp/443 was restored all three read uploaded, with nobody retrying them. They were then read back through a second machine's mount of the same drive -- the Fedora VM, not the daemon that uploaded them -- and all three carried their exact contents. A file the uploading daemon calls done is not evidence; a file another machine can read is.
observed.Q3: HOLDS. stuck_changes stayed 0 from the moment the files were written to the moment they finished. The one failed upload throughout is the pre-existing power-cut file from 2026-09-13, unrelated. An upload waiting for a provider is pending, not stuck, and reporting it as stuck would send someone to discard work that was about to succeed.
observed.Q4: HOLDS, both halves. The upgrade left the daemon on pid 2491, so the queue was carried by the same process -- the restart_required behaviour measured on Fedora, seen again here. Then the daemon was deliberately restarted onto the new binary while the three were still queued: new pid 5316, and all six journal entries still present. The queue survives both a package upgrade and the process restart the upgrade implies.

result.cleanup: All three check files were removed to the provider's recycle bin afterwards; none is left on the drive.
